document_meta.title: New Hampshire State Wildlife Action Plan 2025-2035

orientation.summary: This is the 2025 New Hampshire State Wildlife Action Plan (NH SWAP), a state-level SWAP covering 2025–2035, produced by the NH Fish and Game Department. The document addresses the eight federally required SWAP elements, identifying 326 SGCN, 28 key habitat types, threats, and conservation actions. Climate change is treated as a major threat (third most frequent overall) but the document's posture is descriptive and threat-focused rather than deeply analytical about range shift science. Range shifts are acknowledged, especially in the climate change threats section, with references to species shifting elevation and latitude and species tracking temperature. The document references the Northeast Climate Adaptation Science Center Regional Climate Synthesis (Karmalkar et al., 2024) for climate projections and explicitly discusses climate refugia, connectivity, and climate-adaptive planning but does not perform original range-shift modeling; it primarily incorporates findings from external sources.

evidence_index.text: Watchlist: These are species that are presently secure in New Hampshire but are of concern elsewhere in the Northeast. Many of these species are suspected to be at risk due to emerging threats, such as climate change, that are affecting populations more strongly to our south.

New Hampshire will continue to experience increasing temperatures, with an estimated warming of 7°F (relative to the current climate) by the end of the century (Karmalkar et al., 2024). Given this, by 2100, the number of days during which the maximum daytime temperature is above 95°F is projected to increase roughly ten-fold.
The Gulf of Maine is one of the fastest warming ocean regions in the world and has warmed faster than 99 percent of the global ocean (Gulf of Maine Research Institute, 2024).
New Hampshire and the surrounding ecoregions are projected to experience up to a 50 percent increase in precipitation relative to the current climate (Karmalkar et al., 2024).

Predicting how species will respond to the changing climate depends on two things: how climate will change in the long- and short-term future, and how target species may directly respond to changing temperature and precipitation patterns, as well as indirect abiotic and biotic changes (Karmalkar et al., 2024).
Future projections estimate that as many as 14-32 percent of all species may go extinct by ~2085 (Wiens & Zelinka, 2024).
Similarly, the warming temperatures and phenological shifts driven by climate change can increase disease vulnerability for many species, as is discussed in Appendix N.
